content:
A short argument against the Quran's account of Iblis circulates in Christian polemic. Its steps are simple.

The Quran says God commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam. It also says Iblis "was of the jinn" (18:50), and the jinn are a different order from the angels. So, the argument runs, the command was never addressed to Iblis, and God condemned him for breaking an order that did not include him.

The argument adds two further charges. Angels cannot disobey (66:6), so when they bowed to a creature they committed shirk, associating partners with God, because they had no choice. And Iblis tells God, "Because You have put me in error" (7:16), which the critic reads as proof that God deceived him.

Each step quotes a real verse. The eight answers below take the argument at full strength and test it against the Quran's own wording, the classical commentators and the Bible the critics hold as their standard.

The verses are quoted correctly. God says to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrate, "except for Iblees" (2:34; 7:11; 15:30-31; 17:61; 20:116; 38:73-74). One of those passages adds that Iblis "was of the jinn and departed from the command of his Lord" (18:50).

The Quran also describes angels who "do not disobey God in what He commands them but do what they are commanded" (66:6). A sound hadith in Sahih Muslim gives the three origins: "The angels were created from light, the jinn were created from a smokeless flame of fire, and Adam was created from what has been described to you."[1]

The verses are quoted correctly, then. Muslim scholars read "of the jinn" in two ways, and answer 4 sets both out.

One view is al-Hasan al-Basri's: "Iblis was never one of the angels for the blink of an eye." Ibn Kathir calls the chain of that report sound.[2]

The argument still needs one more premise: that the command was addressed to the angels alone. The Quran settles that premise in so many words.

After the refusal, God speaks to Iblis directly: "What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?" (7:12). The Arabic is idh amartuka, "when I commanded you", with the pronoun in the singular, addressed to Iblis himself.

The same question appears in a second passage, again in the second person: "O Iblees, what prevented you from prostrating to that which I created with My hands?" (38:75).

And 18:50, the verse the objection rests on, says that Iblis "departed from the command of his Lord". A person cannot depart from a command that was never given to him.

The verse the critics quote most, 2:34, ends the same way. Iblis "refused and was arrogant and became of the disbelievers".

All three verbs have Iblis as their subject. A reader who takes that verse as evidence has to take its last clause too.

The objection reads "We said to the angels" as a complete list of who was addressed. The Quran then reports God telling Iblis that the command was his. The critic must choose between his inference and the text.

If the command had been addressed to others, Iblis had a perfect defence. He could have said, "You spoke to the angels, and I am not one of them."

He says something else. "I am better than him.

You created me from fire and created him from clay" (7:12; 38:76). In another passage: "Should I prostrate to one You created from clay?" (17:61).

His answer accepts that the command reached him and argues that it was beneath him. The Quran names the sin in the same verses: he "refused and was arrogant" (2:34). The objection credits Iblis with a defence he never made, and the defence he did make is a claim of superiority by birth.

The gym analogy the critics offer, an instructor who tells the men to do push-ups and then blames a woman in the room, fails on this point. In the Quran's account the instructor turns to her and says, "I told you too," and she answers, "I am better than them."

The classical commentators asked the critic's question centuries ago, and they answered it in two ways. Al-Qurtubi sets out both.[3]

Most of the early authorities he names held that Iblis was one of the angels: Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Jurayj, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Qatadah. On this view "jinn" in 18:50 names a class of angels, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr is reported saying that the jinn were a tribe of the angels created from fire.

Al-Qurtubi notes that al-Tabari preferred this view. Then the exception in "except Iblis" is joined to the group (muttasil), and the objection has nothing to stand on.

The second view, held by al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and others, makes Iblis the father of the jinn. Shahr ibn Hawshab described him as a jinn taken captive young, who "worshipped with the angels and was addressed" with them. Then the exception stands apart from the group (munqati'), and the command still reached him.

Ibn Kathir, commenting on 2:34, writes that when God commanded the angels to prostrate, "Iblis was included in their address, because, although he was not of their substance, he had imitated them and taken on their ways; so he was included in the address to them, and blamed for disobeying the command."[4]

He repeats the point on 18:50. Iblis had taken on the acts of the angels, worshipped as they did and lived among them, "so he was included in their address, and he disobeyed by going against it."[5]

Arabic allows this. A command addressed to a gathering by the name of its larger group reaches everyone present in it, and 7:12 confirms that it reached Iblis. On both of the classical readings, the command was his.

The second charge is that the angels committed shirk by bowing to a creature. That treats every prostration as worship. The Quran does not.

The prostration was a gesture of honour, made on God's order. Al-Qurtubi records that the scholars disagreed about its form "after agreeing that it was not a prostration of worship", and that it was "an honour to Adam and a display of his rank, and obedience to God".[6] Ibn Kathir calls it "a prostration of honour, esteem and respect".[7]

The Quran gives a second example. When Joseph's parents and brothers came to him in Egypt, "they bowed to him in prostration" (12:100), and the Quran presents it as the fulfilment of his dream. No one in that scene worshipped Joseph.

Shirk is giving to a creature what belongs to God. Doing what God commands is the opposite.

The angels bowed because God told them to, so their act was obedience to Him. Iblis refused what God told him, so his act was disobedience to Him. That is the whole contrast the Quran draws.

The objection calls the Quran's account a garbled version of a Jewish and Christian story. That story deserves a look.

In the Life of Adam and Eve, a Jewish and Christian work older than the Quran, Satan explains his fall. He says that Michael brought Adam before the angels and commanded them to worship him as the image of God, that Michael worshipped first, and that Satan refused because Adam was created after him and stood lower than him.[8]

So the older story also has a command to bow to Adam, and in it the word is worship. On the critic's own standard, that story has God's angels commit shirk by divine order. The Quran's version removes the problem: it calls the act sujud, prostration, and the commentators state that it was never worship.

The New Testament goes further. Hebrews applies to Jesus the line "Let all the angels of God worship him" (Hebrews 1:6).

Christians read that as fitting, since they hold Jesus to be divine. The point here is narrower. A critic who calls any bow before a created figure shirk has to apply the charge to the texts he holds sacred before he applies it to the Quran.

The third charge rests on Iblis's words: "Because You have put me in error, I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path" (7:16), and "My Lord, because You have put me in error, I will surely make [disobedience] attractive to them on earth" (15:39).

These are the words of the accused, reported by the Quran. The Quran reports many claims so as to answer them, including Pharaoh's claim to be the highest lord (79:24). Reporting a claim leaves it to be judged.

Al-Tabari glosses the verb aghwaytani as "You have led me astray", from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd, and notes a second sense, "You have destroyed me".[9] Sunni scholars read the verse as Iblis acknowledging God's decree over his fate, a decree they always held together with the creature's own responsibility. And the order of events in the Quran matters: Iblis refused and was asked why.

He gave his reason, and only then was he expelled. His complaint comes after his choice.

God's reply in the same passage names the cause of the sentence: "Descend from Paradise, for it is not for you to be arrogant therein" (7:13). Iblis was judged for the pride he had already shown in front of the whole assembly. Nothing in the account suggests a trap laid for him before that moment, and the Quran gives his own words as the evidence against him.

The Quran states the principle elsewhere: "And when they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate" (61:5). Being left in error is the consequence of a choice already made, and Iblis's choice was made in front of God, with the command in his ears.

The Bible says the same kind of thing about God, in stronger words. God hardens Pharaoh's heart (Exodus 9:12).

God puts "a lying spirit" in the mouths of Ahab's prophets (1 Kings 22:23). Paul writes that God "sends them a working of error, that they should believe a lie" (2 Thessalonians 2:11). A critic who reads 7:16 as divine deceit must read these the same way.

The charge ends by calling Iblis "just another victim". The Quran gives Satan the last word on that question, on the Day of Judgement.

"And Satan will say when the matter has been concluded, 'Indeed, God had promised you the promise of truth. And I promised you, but I betrayed you.

But I had no authority over you except that I invited you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me; but blame yourselves'" (14:22).

The same rule binds Iblis. God tells him, "Indeed, My servants, no authority will you have over them, except those who follow you of the deviators" (15:42).

Iblis can invite. He cannot compel.

Surah al-Nahl gives the same rule in plain terms: "Indeed, there is for him no authority over those who have believed and rely upon their Lord. His authority is only over those who take him as an ally" (16:99-100). Iblis's reach depends on the choice of the one he invites, exactly as his own fall depended on his choice at the command. And he was answerable for his own refusal, as every creature with a will is answerable.

Al-Faruqi made this the meaning of the trust in 33:72. Nature does God's will by necessity; the creature that can refuse is the one whose obedience counts, and whose refusal counts too.[10] The jinn were created, like humans, "except to worship Me" (51:56). Iblis had the freedom the angels did not, and he used it to refuse.

The bottom line

The objection needs the command to Adam to exclude Iblis. The Quran says the reverse in God's own words, "when I commanded you" (7:12), and Iblis's reply admits it. The commentators explain why: he stood among the angels, took on their ways, and was addressed with them.

The prostration was honour to Adam and obedience to God, as the commentators agree and as the bowing of Joseph's family shows. The words "because You have put me in error" are the plea of the accused, made after his refusal, and Satan withdraws it himself on the Day of Judgement.

The site's article on whether God deceives, Is Allah a deceiver? 7 answers on makr, takes up the wider charge, and the article on Iblis and the fallen-angel legends compares the Quran's account with the older stories. God knows best.

Notes

  1. Sahih Muslim 2996, report of 'A'ishah; graded sahih in the Dorar hadith encyclopedia (dorar.net). Quran translations in this article follow Saheeh International, with "God" for "Allah".
  2. Ibn Kathir, Tafsir al-Quran al-'Azim, ed. Sami Salamah (Riyadh: Dar Tayba, 1999), 1:230–231, on Quran 2:34, citing al-Tabari's report from 'Awf from al-Hasan: ما كان إبليس من الملائكة طرفة عين قط. Checked against the Shamela text of this edition.
  3. Al-Qurtubi, al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran, ed. Ahmad al-Barduni and Ibrahim Atfish (Cairo: Dar al-Kutub al-Misriyyah, 2nd ed., 1964), 1:293–294, on Quran 2:34, the fifth point: نصب على الاستثناء المتصل، لأنه كان من الملائكة على قول الجمهور and, for the second view, وتعبد مع الملائكة وخوطب … والاستثناء على هذا منقطع. Checked against the Shamela text of this edition.
  4. Ibn Kathir, Tafsir, 1:229–230, on Quran 2:34: دخل إبليس في خطابهم؛ لأنه -وإن لم يكن من عنصرهم- إلا أنه كان قد تشبه بهم وتوسم بأفعالهم.
  5. Ibn Kathir, Tafsir, 5:166–167, on Quran 18:50.
  6. Al-Qurtubi, al-Jami', 1:292–293, on Quran 2:34, the fourth point: بعد اتفاقهم على أنه لم يكن سجود عبادة.
  7. Ibn Kathir, Tafsir, 5:166–167, on Quran 18:50: سجود تشريف وتكريم وتعظيم.
  8. Life of Adam and Eve (Latin Vita Adae et Evae) 13–16, trans. M. D. Johnson, in James H. Charlesworth, ed., The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha, vol. 2 (Garden City, NY: Doubleday, 1985). Bible quotations in this article are from the World English Bible.
  9. Al-Tabari, Jami' al-Bayan, ed. 'Abd Allah al-Turki (Cairo: Dar Hajr, 2001), 10:90–91, on Quran 7:16; checked against the Shamela text of this edition.
  10. Ismail Raji al-Faruqi, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life, 2nd edition (Herndon: International Institute of Islamic Thought, 1992), chapter 1, on the trust of 33:72.
